paragraphs.text: Every German noun has a gender, and the article in front of it tells your listener something about the thing itself, not just about the grammar. When you introduce a place for the first time, you are pointing at something your listener does not yet know — so German uses the indefinite article: ein, ein or eine.
Das ist ein Hafen. · Das ist ein Hotel. · Das ist eine Straße. · Das sind Schiffe.

The moment the thing is identified — named, pointed out, agreed on by both of you — the article changes. German switches to the definite set: der for masculine, das for neuter, die for feminine and also for the plural. The choice is not decoration; it is the difference between a thing you are introducing and a thing you both already see.
Das ist der Hafen von Hamburg. · Das Hotel heißt »Alster«. · Die Straße heißt Müllerstraße. · Die Schiffe sind im Hafen.

blocks.englishBridge: The two sets mark the same difference English makes with a and the, but in German the article also carries the noun's gender, so ein, eine and the der/das/die trio belong together as one system.

paragraphs.text: Before you drill the articles, spend two minutes on the sounds of this page. German vowels are either long or short, and the length is part of the word: a stretched vowel in {{de:Hafen}}, a clipped one in {{de:Fluss}}. Listeners use that length to tell words apart, so it is worth hearing deliberately while you practise.

One clue works in one direction, and there it is reliable. Before a double consonant — ff, nn, ss and friends — the vowel is always short: {{de:Schiff}}, {{de:Fluss}}. In words without one, the vowel usually stretches: {{de:Hafen}}, {{de:See}}, {{de:Turm}}. Say the pairs out loud once — the contrast is easier to hear than to explain.
Kurz: Schiff · Bus · Fluss · Rathaus. Lang: Hafen · See · Turm · Zug.
